cues.text: Welcome to our first recorded mathematics class.
A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of entries, with rows running across and
columns running down.
Its order is the number of rows followed by the number of columns.
A matrix with two rows and three columns has order two by three, even though
it
contains six entries.
The entry a sub i j lies in row i and column j.
Equality requires equal orders and equality at every corresponding position.
A row matrix has one row; a column matrix has one column.
A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns.
Its main diagonal joins positions with equal row and column indices.
In a diagonal matrix, all entries outside that diagonal are zero.
Diagonal entries themselves may also be zero.
A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix with every diagonal entry equal
to the same scalar. The identity matrix has diagonal entries one and all other
entries zero.
Every identity matrix is scalar, but a scalar matrix with diagonal entry two
is
not an identity.
A zero matrix has every entry zero and need not be square.
Before any calculation, write the order and check the defining condition.
A name such as square describes structure, not whether an inverse exists.
Matrix addition pairs corresponding entries, so the two matrices must have the
same order.
Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry.
Multiplying a two by two matrix by three changes its entries, not its order.
Transposition exchanges rows with columns.
If A has order m by n, its transpose has order n by m, and the entry at row i
column j becomes the entry at row j column i.
Transposing twice returns the original matrix.
Transposition distributes over addition and scalar multiplication.
A real square matrix is symmetric when its transpose equals itself.
It is skew symmetric when its transpose is the negative of itself.
For a skew symmetric real matrix, each diagonal entry equals its own negative
and therefore must be zero.
The zero diagonal alone is not sufficient: opposite off diagonal entries must
also have opposite signs.
Every real square matrix can be decomposed into a symmetric part and a skew
symmetric part.
Take half the sum with its transpose for the symmetric part, and half the
difference for the skew symmetric part.
Adding those parts restores A.
For A with rows one, three and one, two, the symmetric part has rows one, two
and two, two.
The skew part has rows zero, one and negative one, zero.
This decomposition preserves the order and can be checked entry by entry.
Matrix multiplication combines a row of the first matrix with a column of the
second.
Multiply corresponding entries along that row and column, then add the
products.
A matrix of order m by n can multiply one of order n by p, producing a matrix
of order m by p.
The inner dimensions agree and the outer dimensions remain.
With A having rows one, two and zero, one, and B having rows one, zero and
three, one, calculate the first entry of A B.
It is one times one plus two times three, giving seven.
The complete product has rows seven, two and three, one.
Reverse the order and B A has rows one, two and three, seven.
Thus both products exist but differ.
Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive, yet it is generally not
commutative.
Even a product equal to the zero matrix does not force one factor to be zero.
For example, the diagonal matrices with diagonals one, zero and zero, one have
zero product.
In a transpose of a product, reverse the factor order: the transpose of A B is
B transpose times A transpose.
Finally, A X equals A Y does not permit cancellation unless A is known to be
invertible.
Always check order, compute row by column, and justify any cancellation.
For a two by two matrix with first row a, b and second row c, d, the
determinant is a d minus b c.
It is a scalar, not a new matrix.
With rows two, one and five, three, the determinant is six minus five, or one.
Determinants are defined here for square matrices; do not assign this formula
to a rectangular array.
Several properties make larger evaluations faster.
Swapping two rows changes the determinant sign.
Multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k.
Adding a multiple of another row to a row leaves the determinant unchanged.
These same statements hold for columns.
Equal or proportional rows give determinant zero.
A triangular matrix has determinant equal to the product of its diagonal
entries.
Transposing a matrix preserves its determinant, and the determinant of a
product equals the product of the determinants.
Be careful with scaling the whole matrix.
In an n by n matrix, multiplying every entry by k scales all n rows, so the
determinant is multiplied by k to the power n.
For a two by two matrix the factor is k squared, not k.
Finally, determinants are not generally additive: the determinant of A plus B
is not generally the sum of their determinants.
A minor is the determinant left after deleting a specified row and column.
A cofactor attaches the sign negative one to the power i plus j to that minor.
The first cofactor sign row is plus, minus, plus.
The second is minus, plus, minus.
To expand a determinant along a row, multiply each row entry by its own
cofactor and add.
Choose a row or column containing zeros when possible.
Consider A with rows one, one, zero; zero, one, one; and one, zero, one.
Expand along its first row.
The first minor is one times one minus one times zero, giving one.
The second minor is zero times one minus one times one, giving negative one.
Its cofactor sign is negative, so the second cofactor is positive one.
The determinant is one times one plus one times one plus zero, giving two.
A common mistake is to apply the negative sign twice or forget it entirely.
An independent check is useful: subtract the first row from the third,
producing third row zero, negative one, one, without changing the determinant.
Expansion along the first column then gives two again.
Determinant preserving row additions simplify evaluation, but swapping or
scaling rows requires tracking the corresponding factor or sign.
The adjoint, also called the adjugate, is the transpose of the cofactor
matrix.
The transpose step matters: writing cofactors in their original positions
generally does not give the adjoint.
Multiplying a square matrix by its adjoint, in either order, gives its
determinant times the identity.
Consequently, a matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
Divide its adjoint by that determinant.
For a two by two matrix, swap the two diagonal entries and negate the other
two
entries to obtain its adjoint.
For A with rows two, one and five, three, the determinant is one, so its
inverse has rows three, negative one and negative five, two.
Multiplying A by that proposed inverse gives rows one, zero and zero, one.
For our three by three example with rows one, one, zero; zero, one, one; and
one, zero, one, the adjoint has rows one, negative one, one; one, one,
negative
one; and negative one, one, one.
Its inverse is half that array because the determinant is two.
A zero determinant does not mean the adjoint is always zero, and division by
zero is never an inverse formula.
Also, the inverse of A B is B inverse times A inverse when both inverses
exist.
Put B inverse first and A inverse second.
Check the factor order before simplifying a product inverse.
A system of linear equations becomes A X equals B when each row of A contains
the coefficients in the same variable order.
For two x plus y equals five and five x plus three y equals thirteen, choose X
as the column x, y.
A has rows two, one and five, three, and B has entries five, thirteen.
The determinant is one, so a unique solution exists.
Multiply the inverse of A on the left of both sides.
This gives X equals A inverse times B, not B times A inverse.
Using inverse rows three, negative one and negative five, two, the first
component is fifteen minus thirteen, giving x equal to two.
The second is negative twenty five plus twenty six, giving y equal to one.
Substitute: two times two plus one equals five, and five times two plus three
times one equals thirteen.
Both equations check.
A missing variable contributes coefficient zero; it does not remove its
column.
If an equation is written with constants on both sides, collect variable terms
and constants before building the matrix.
The inverse method is available only after checking the determinant is
nonzero.
A zero determinant sends us to consistency analysis rather than allowing us to
conclude automatically that there is no solution.
Now take three equations: x plus y equals three; y plus z equals five;
and x plus z equals four.
In variable order x, y, z, the coefficient matrix has rows one, one, zero;
zero, one, one; and one, zero, one.
The constant column has entries three, five, four.
We already evaluated the coefficient determinant as two, so the inverse
exists.
Its adjoint has rows one, negative one, one; one, one, negative one; and
negative one, one, one.
Multiply that adjoint by the constant column before dividing by two.
The first component is three minus five plus four, giving two; after division,
x is one.
The second is three plus five minus four, giving four; hence y is two.
The third is negative three plus five plus four, giving six; hence z is three.
Verify all three original equations: one plus two is three, two plus three is
five, and one plus three is four.
A useful independent solution is to add the first and third equations and
subtract the second, obtaining two x equals two.
This agrees with the matrix method.
The point of the inverse calculation is to organize a systematic method, not
to
forbid a shorter check.
When a parameter enters a coefficient, identify determinant zero cases before
dividing by its expression.
A zero determinant means the coefficient matrix is singular.
It does not by itself distinguish no solution from infinitely many solutions.
Compare x plus y equals two with two x plus two y equals four.
Subtract twice the first equation from the second and obtain zero equals zero.
The second equation is redundant.
Set y equal to a free real parameter t and x equal to two minus t; infinitely
many pairs solve both equations.
Change the second constant to five and the same subtraction gives zero equals
one.
This is a contradiction, so no solution exists.
The coefficient determinants are identical in these two examples.
For three variables, consider x plus y plus z equals three; x minus y plus z
equals one; and two x plus two z equals four.
The third equation is the sum of the first two.
Subtracting the second equation from the first gives y equal to one, leaving x
plus z equals two.
Thus x equals two minus t and z equals t is an infinite solution family.
Replacing the last constant four with five creates a contradiction after
subtracting the first two equations from the third.
Row reduction must act on the augmented matrix, including constants.
Inspect the exceptional values of a parameter separately; a vanished
denominator is a warning to analyze the original equations.
Check their constants for a contradiction or a free variable before
classifying
the solution set.
For three points in a plane, place their x coordinate, y coordinate and one in
successive rows of a three by three determinant.
Half its absolute value is the triangle area.
The determinant itself is an oriented quantity: swapping two points reverses
its sign, while the geometric area remains unchanged.
For the points zero, zero; four, zero; and zero, three, expansion gives
determinant twelve and area six square units.
Subtracting the first point from the others reduces the same calculation to
half the absolute value of a two by two determinant of the displacement
vectors.
If the determinant is zero, the three points are collinear or include repeated
points, and the triangle is degenerate.
For points one, two; three, four; and five, k, the determinant simplifies to
two k minus twelve.
Collinearity therefore requires k equal to six.
Finish by connecting determinant tests across the class.
The matrix with rows lambda, one and one, lambda has determinant lambda
squared
minus one.
It is invertible for all real lambda except plus one and minus one.
At an exceptional value, a linear system needs its constants checked for
consistency.
Determinants summarize important information, but zero area, a singular
coefficient matrix and inconsistency are different conclusions attached to
different questions.
Name the question, compute the determinant, and interpret it in context.
